newsitem.title: CHINA: HK cleans up, returning to normal after big storm.
newsitem.headline: HK cleans up, returning to normal after big storm.

text.p: Hong Kong cleaned up on Sunday after one of the most powerful typhoons in years slammed into the territory overnight, killing one man and injuring at least 55 others.

Typhoon Victor left a trail of debris in its wake as it lashed Hong Kong with heavy rains and powerful winds, sending residents scurrying home and turning the busy Central District into a virtual ghost town by Saturday evening.

It scored a direct hit on the territory and the number nine typhoon signal, which indicates winds of more than 118 km per hour (73 mph), was hoisted for the first time since 1983. At one stage on Saturday night, an eerie calm descended as the eye of the storm enveloped the territory.

All storm warning signals were lowered by dawn on Sunday as Victor moved north away from Hong Kong to southern China's Guangdong province. At 11:00 a.m. (0300 GMT) it was centred 300 km (188 miles) north of the provincial capital and was forecast to move further north, gradually dissipating over land, the Hong Kong Observatory said.
Better weather prompted people to venture outside on Sunday, but the streets were a far cry from the usual crowd of shoppers and diners, although many malls and restaurants began to re-open.
One man, Tom Larmour, a 44-year-old Briton, drowned after trying to save two men who were swept into the sea at Stanley on southern Hong Kong Island at the height of the typhoon on Saturday night.

Witnesses said Larmour, who had been drinking in one of the bars near the sea, jumped into the water to try to rescue the two men but all three were pounded against a seawall by high waves. The other two were eventually saved.
The storm caused 12 landslips and at least 33 flooding incidents, a government spokeswoman told Reuters on Sunday.

Strong winds tore down building scaffolding and signboards and uprooted a number of trees. Floods in parts of the territory forced vehicles and pedestrians to wade through water and inundated many vegetable fields.

Air traffic was still affected on Sunday, with some cancellations and delays following major disruptions on Saturday that forced hundreds of passengers to spend the night at Kai Tak International Airport.

By dawn on Sunday Victor had affected 322 flights, including cancellations, delays and diversions, the government said in a statement. The number of disrupted flights on Sunday morning was not immediately available.
Land and sea traffic, which had ground to a halt by Saturday night, gradually returned to normal although some services were still suspended or diverted.
Some roads, including the huge Tsing Ma suspension bridge -- a major Hong Kong landmark linking Lantau Island to the Kowloon peninsula -- was re-opened after being closed on Saturday.
But some roads were jammed by container trucks flocking to container terminals which had partially resumed services.
Four people were missing in the neighbouring Chinese town of Shenzhen after the typhoon swept through, local television said on Sunday.
